lesson.title: Not All Packets Are Created Equal: The Case for Quality of Service
lesson.summary: Quality of Service (QoS) is the general problem of managing a network's limited capacity so that traffic gets the bandwidth, delay, jitter, and loss behavior it actually needs, instead of every packet being treated identically.
lesson.body:
The original Internet Protocol was built around best-effort delivery: routers forward packets in whatever order they arrive, drop them when queues fill up, and make no promise about when, or even whether, a given packet arrives. For a huge amount of traffic this is completely fine. Web pages, email, and file downloads are handled by the transport layer's reliability mechanisms, covered earlier, which retransmit whatever gets lost, so the application eventually gets a perfect copy even if a few packets took a slow or bumpy route to get there.

Real-time interactive traffic breaks that assumption. A voice call or a video conference cares less about eventually receiving a perfect copy of every packet and more about receiving packets promptly and at a steady pace. A voice packet that arrives four seconds late is not merely late, it is useless, because the moment in the conversation it belonged to has already been played through as silence or filled with a guess. This is the underlying reason QoS exists as a distinct problem: some traffic is delay-tolerant and some is not, and a network that treats both identically will serve the delay-intolerant traffic worse than it needs to, purely because nothing is telling routers to do otherwise.

QoS is usually described along four measurable dimensions. Bandwidth is how much data per second a flow can push through. Latency is how long a single packet takes to arrive. Jitter is the variation in that latency from one packet to the next, which matters because a receiver typically uses a small playout buffer to smooth audio or video, and if delay swings around unpredictably that buffer either runs dry or overflows. Packet loss is simply how much data never arrives at all. Different applications weight these differently: a large file transfer cares mostly about bandwidth and can tolerate latency and even some jitter, while a voice call cares intensely about latency and jitter and can often tolerate a small amount of loss better than it can tolerate lateness.

QoS does not create more bandwidth out of nothing. What it does is make deliberate choices, at points of congestion, about which traffic waits and which does not. The rest of this unit works through the actual toolbox that makes those choices concrete: traffic shaping controls how bursty a flow's output looks as it enters the network, token bucket and leaky bucket are two specific algorithms for doing that shaping, fair queuing and scheduling disciplines control the order packets leave a shared link once they are queued, admission control decides whether a network should accept new demand at all, and DiffServ and IntServ are two different, real, historically significant architectures for how priority gets signaled and enforced across an entire path rather than just at one router. It is also worth connecting this back to the transport layer prerequisite: TCP's congestion control already reacts to loss and delay by backing off, which is a kind of self-imposed fairness, but it is enforced by the endpoints at the edge of the network, voluntarily. QoS mechanisms are what the network itself, at the routers in the middle, actively does regardless of whether an endpoint cooperates.
